raw.description:
Loopy captures a kind of bubbly lettershapes that are familiar from comics, stickers and street art, but rarely seen in serious typography, and thus rarely given the attention to detail that they deserve. Systematically irregular, with sometimes looping outlines, Loopy is happily ignorant about logic or typographic etiquette.

It's a layered color typeface. You can combine styles with outline, highlight, shadow and fill, and set them in any colors you like.

You can do whatever. Do an invitation card, typeset a bible.

Loopy is free software and open source.

The »Basalt« typeface itself was a simplified version of the »Ege-Schrift«, also designed by Eduard Ege in 1921 and published by Genzsch & Heyse. Initially, both typefaces were exclusively all-caps. In 1934, »Basalt« was enhanced with a lowercase alphabet, which has unfortunately been largely lost to time. The only surviving example of the lowercase letters is found in a flyer distributed in the Netherlands during World War II, showcasing the letters a, c, g, h, i, n, r, s, u, and w. Drawing inspiration from the design principles of these surviving letters, type designer Lena Schmidt crafted the remaining lowercase letters, resulting in a complete alphabet.

Zick Zack S&B is a dynamic display typeface that seamlessly blends vibrancy and coolness while maintaining a non-intrusive presence. Its expressive form creates a powerful visual statement, making it ideal for display applications. Perfect for headlines, posters, packaging, playful editorial layouts, and engaging visual systems, this typeface excels in bold and energetic compositions. Designed for striking visual impact rather than neutrality, Zick Zack S&B ensures that every design possesses a unique voice, enhancing the overall aesthetic appeal.

Peridot Tamil is a multifaceted 20-style sans serif type system by Foundry5. It comes in 10 weights and matching italic styles, in static and variable format. Loaded with personality, the diverse range of widths and styles in Peridot offers a dynamic typographic toolbox, ready to inspire and captivate even the most innovative designers.

Peridot Tamil supports Tamil and Latin and covers over 314 languages. Peridot performs in varied environments – from branding, display, corporate use,  editorial, advertising, poster, web, screen usage etc. It is the gem you ought to have in your collection.

Comma Serif is the final chapter of the Comma trilogy, a superfamily of three closely connected typefaces (Base, Sans, & Serif), each with its own voice. Where Base sets the personality, Sans pairs expressive character with formal geometric stroke endings. Comma Serif carries the warmth and angularity of Comma Base, while adding strong serifs, classical proportions, and a true italic with calligraphic details. Its powerful uniwidth design is highly valued by designers who switch weights without disturbing the flow. Comma Serif is a workhorse with character!

The capitals of the Blackletter, or Fraktur genre perplex modern readers, familiar as we are with the letter forms of Ancient Rome, epitomized on Trajan’s column. 

With legibility in mind, type designers have, over the years, created hybrid Fraktur capitals, Romanized to varying degrees, and such is the case with Puffery, quite thoroughly in fact—more so than in other variants of the “Old English” genre. Consequently, one of the more exotic Textura styles becomes perfectly acceptable for all-cap settings.

There is also a Vintage Capitals version of Puffery, with the classic capitals, so that the relative merits of authenticity and readability may be addressed, according to the job in hand.

What does a typeface for knowledge work look today? We investigated. The result: knowledge needs to be branded.
A knowledge worker’s font needs to convey trust, poise, and elegance. It must be recognizable but never distracting as soon as you start reading. This is what we sought to achieve with our Foliant superfamily.
Foliant Serif is a text face with a tilted axis and flat, unbracketed serifs. It excels at body copy and immersive reading. In large sizes, its crisp details kick in, giving titles and headlines an erudite appeal.
All styles of Foliant Serif work well with the corresponding weights of Foliant Sans. They’ll have the same color and similar proportions. 10 weights, 900+ glpyhs.

Cyclops is a typeface full of character, perfectly suited for packaging, games and campaigns. Its smooth curves create a warm vibe and its overall compactness and fixed height make it perfect for tight type setting with a homogenous line height. Even the accents are implemented into the letter-height to keep the overall line height consistent.

The Match type family is a versatile tool with a broad scope of tonalities — The strong, confident and loud Ultra and Black styles. On the other end are the elegant Thin and Light styles. In between are the more silent and strong workers, delivering a good performance for reading texts.

A knowledge worker’s font needs to convey trust, poise, and elegance. It must be recognizable but never distracting as soon as you start reading. This is what we sought to achieve with our Foliant superfamily.

Foliant Sans is a humanist sans-serif typeface with a geometric look and dynamically angled stroke endings. It’s approachable, legible, sincere.

The default version mirrors the classic letterforms of Foliant Serif for optimum legibility and character distinction. Foliant Sans Modern is simpler, for a more graphic brand appeal in larger sizes. 20 weights, 1000+ characters.

Gurky Grotesque is a type family consisting of 12 fonts, ranging from ExtraLight to Black. It is reminiscent of old metal type, favoring quirky imperfections over smooth curves. We went on a search for character and unique solutions to bring back the charm of vernacular type and the appeal of imperfection. In contrast to big type systems without irregularities, Gurky Grotesque embraces its inconsistencies and its edginess. It comes with a comprehensive character set and modern OpenType features.

Say “Hi” to the narrow addition to the Mikado Family: Mikado Condensed. Space Saving, powerful, easy and fun – the letterforms are innocent and easygoing on the one hand and prepared for professional typographic challenges on the other hand. A big character set, good spacing & kerning and screen optimised fonts make Mikado and Mikado Condensed a good choice for professional usage for games, toys or ice cream.

Cabrio is a humanist sans serif type family that combines geometric shapes with subtle, but playful details of a script typeface. Letters with character as well as an overall compact appearance of the heavier weights lend Cabrio a strong recognisability, especially in larger sizes. Open letterforms and a large x-height make it a useful companion for both long copy and short texts. Cabrio makes a clear and professional impression and, paired with a human element, it offers a convincing solution for corporate designs and advertising.

Explore Officer Sans – the perfect typeface for your office.
Type design is about more than crafting beautiful letters. In your day-to-day business, you don’t need flashy and fashionable — you need fonts that will always get the job done, a typographic workhorse. Officer Sans is a beautifully crafted and highly functional all-rounder font family perfectly suited to the modern office environment and designed to the most exacting typographic standards. It looks great too!

Finlay Sans is the “sans-swash” version of supertype’s script typeface Finlay. With its slightly curved strokes and rounded ends, it retains some of the characteristics associated with writing, giving it a warmer and more lively feel than your typical sans-serif.
In smaller sizes, its open, humanist letterforms and large x-height make it easy and comfortable to read, even for the youngest audiences. In larger sizes, the friendly design works beautifully on packaging, in print, or even on signage, especially for anything rustic, handmade, healthy, or fun. With seven weights, it offers plenty of room for typographic contrasts and to create clear hierarchy in your design.

Talaris presents itself as a softly blurred, subtly overlaid grotesque with flowing transitions and deliberately softened contours.
Formally, the typeface recalls the experimental digital culture of the 1990s and stands in clear proximity to Emigre and Fuse fonts, where imperfection was embraced as a deliberate design attitude.
In contrast to its historical predecessors, Talaris appears more controlled and systematic, guided by a clear typographic logic.
With 12 styles and support for 144 languages, the typeface offers a high degree of flexibility for a wide range of typographic applications.
Talaris bridges the spirit of the digital avant-garde of the 1990s with contemporary usability in editorial, branding, and conceptual design.

Zoo is a strong and high contrast display typeface. The inspiration comes from the lettering raised on the vinyl sleeves of a french jazz music band called « Zoo ». The two letters « Z » & « O » established the construction constraints of the design of the all character set. The asymmetrical distribution of the shapes makes it a dancing typeface family, layouts live through this concept.

Zoo combines sharpness and roundness, delicateness and strength.

Ysans designed by Jean François Porchez is a sans serif influenced by Cassandre lettering pieces and the geometric sanserif style from the inter-war period. Since Chanel logo, the geometric sans serif style has been the favorite typographic thing in fashion. Ysans asserts this reference. Not only Haute-Couture houses use these categories of typefaces for their visual identity, but fashion magazines usually strength their layout with these geometric sanserif when a Didot isn’t used.
Cherry on the cake: Ysans Mondrian. Ysans Mondrian, named in reference to the Mondrian dress created by Yves Saint Laurent, is the display version of the family.

I’ve been doing some deep diving into the strange font ventures of William Morris. So naturally, I decided to create my own interpretation of his pretty darned ugly Roman face. The font is actually “ugly” in many good ways. But, look it up. You’ll see the CAPS. My goals was to amplify the good ugly, and I landed on what is, to my eyes, something very pretty.

WT Morris Roman is based off his Golden produced for fine bookmaking at the Kelmscott Press. That face was based on some early Jenson cuts, but with thicker and more uniform strokes. However, some of the strokes and widths kept by Morris make it mostly unusable. This font is my attempt to reconcile all these things.

The latest addition to my type library is a font which I couldn’t have imagined 3 weeks ago, but boy am I glad that I made it. Much like the original Weathersbee font staple, Franchise, it can play an outrageous number of typographic roles; the difference here is that WT Iron brings the power, the aggression, the energy, and brings the dorky shapes of a sci-fi tech font.

WT Iron is a font whose genesis, like many of my type ventures, lies in the extension of a work-a-day task. In this case, I got a “simple” ask from my brother to cut out WEATHERSBEE for his home gym using my CNC. I hate the bland jersey letter style, but needed to match it while adding a little character to it.

Worldwide is a classic news face that has been used in dozens of newspapers around the world. What makes it special is micro-detailing that is both a means of enhancing the legibility of text and a source of visual interest at headline size. Vertical stems are cinched in the middle, serifs are delicately barbed and acute joints between stems are equipped with ink traps. Such detail has a mannered quality suggestive of the complex trace of process that it addresses.

Make a little extra impact with this strong athletic font with big geometric muscles, clean lines and sharp teeth, too. Originally created for a local pro basketball team in Minnesota, this sporty and big-shoulder poster font is now available directly to you for the first time ever to add some punch to your printed or web designs. Crisp and clear and ready for action a concise variety of weights and styles!
Grunge font based on ink bleed into paper

Witch Hazel has been quite a while in the making; a fun font with slightly flared serifs, lots of ligatures and alternates, and over 1150 glyphs!

This font is great for holiday designs, from Valentine's Day to Halloween to Christmas! It also bridges modern and vintage styling, so you can use it for fairy tales and pirates, or for your company's branding and logo!

For my ILT folks, I've also included the two spurs alphabets in their own font file; just type the lowercase letters and regular numbers for the pointy spurs, and type the uppercase letters and hold down Shift while typing numbers for the rounded spurs!

Plenty of swashes, ligatures, beginning and ending shapes, Wishes is a wit option for invitations, cards, stationery, fashion and apparel, among a wide range of uses. The curves of the cursive style are neither too solemn or pompous, its grace and playfulness are more 1950s than 1750s. This family offers the designer an additional decorative toolkit full of frames, ribbons, hearts, flowers and ornaments, plus a collection of caps and small caps.
Wishes Script Pro includes the complete set of Script characters plus Ornaments and Caps. The family offers optically optimized Display and Text styles for each of the weights: Light, Regular and Bold. Use professional software that support OpenType

Wintler is a workhorse grotesque with a cold straightforward nature and neutral design. Its openness of forms originates from the award-winning Decutto typeface and is adapted for a more universal use. The story of Wintler originates from a cases where designers tried to use the Decutto typeface not only for headings, but also for body text. Well, Decutto wasn't designed for that, because it built on straight simplified forms that looks too crisp in a body text. The goal of Wintler is to preserve the openness of Decutto's forms and gently translate it into a more universal grotesque. Therefore, its letter shape balances between simplified rectangularity and classic roundness.

The script family has a feature set of its own, with initial and final swashes on lowercase letters, middle swashes for select characters, and a titling feature that joins words together by replacing the space with a line. Stylistic alternates create a bouncing baseline on connecting strokes.

Winslow Title is a high contrast modern type family comes in two styles and a monolinear script family. The traditional proportions of Winslow Title are historical in nature and follow the design and style of Winslow Book as a high contrast variant. The Winslow Title Mod family is a contemporary take on the style, with tapering terminals and less pronounced finials. Each family includes both styles, to be accessed through the opentype panel as a stylistic alternate. If preferable, you can purchase the entire family collection to have easier access to both styles, but it's not necessary.

The Winslow Title Mod family is a contemporary take on the style, with tapering terminals and less pronounced finials. Each family includes both styles, to be accessed through the opentype panel as a stylistic alternate. Winslow Book is a playfully modern typeface with 6 weights and packed with styling features. Delicate features give it a playful feel while keeping Scotch Modern attributes of vertical stress, bracket serifs and ball terminals, while unique features give it a personality of its own. Winslow was designed to be a perfect typeface for text and display purposes.

Winslow comes with an array of alternative features that add an extra bit of flair. From stylistic alternatives to tail serifs (in K, k, d, h, m, n) to complete new character designs (for g, y and &) a designer can choose which style they need for any project. Discretionary ligatures also create alternatives to capital pairings.

Winner™ and Winner Sans™—Classic athletic aesthetics, finally as a versatile contemporary super family. Just when you thought there was nothing left to add to the classic sports design, we lifted it to a whole new level. Whatever you want to set in whatever space, with seven weights in seven widths both with or without serifs, you’ll definitely find the right proportions for it! Winner supports not only most Latin-based languages but also Greek. Its extensive character set also contains currency signs, arrows, as well as a wide range of numerals. With more than 24,000 glyphs in 49 fonts, Winner leaves nothing to be desired. Grab Condensed Regular for free and give it a spin!

While conceiving Winco, Ramiro Espinoza studied the work of the masters of postwar book cover design: Helmut Salden, Boudewijn Ietswaart, Berthold Wolpe; among others. He also looked into German and Czech traditions of expressive printing types that had such a strong presence in the earliest decades of the 20th century. Having established a stylistic framework, Espinoza designed the typeface from scratch. The process has resulted in a typeface that successfully combines the high legibility and seriousness of a text face with the expressiveness, dynamism and subtle irreverence of the original hand-rendered alphabets.
Wilko is the carnival barker of typefaces. Bold, impactful yet friendly, with two decorative variants. No frills, no corners, no messing. When you want to say it loud and clear.

Wild Loops is a handwritten monolinear typeface for wild ideas. Inspired by the marker sketches and graffiti on the walls, the font speaks to a young audience and looks a bit crazy with its stretched Ascenders and Descenders. The main feature of the font is a smart Contextual Alternates that substitute different versions of letters depending on its position in the word (at the beginning, middle, and the end of a word), which makes the writing more natural.

The promo images used illustrations from the city walls of Groningen and Wrocław, photos of Cottonbro, Marlene Leppänen, Zhugewala from Pexels, and photos of Kevin Grieve, Liwei Zhang, Nathan Dumlao from Unsplash.

Wilco Loft Sans is an all-caps, high contrast sans serif. We took those handful of letters found on the sign blow molds and expanded those into a full alphabet in 4 weights: Treble, Midrange, Low End, and Bass.

As an easter egg, there's a custom icon for each band member based on a favorite instrument they play at The Loft—in the style of the lefty acoustic found on the original sign. A very special thanks to Spencer Tweedy, who spearheaded this dream project with one of my very favorite artists.

Whiteblack is a slab serif with a soft touch, designed for contemporary typography and comes up with 6 weights for positive and negative settings plus handslanted obliques.
In dark backgrounds, especially for signage and on screen, negative settings glow and appear heavier than positive settings. To avoid the „glow-effect“ the typeface contains special weights for an optimal balance between white and black.
A large x-height and open apertures not only creates space for smaller sizes, but also lends Whiteblack a solid balanced and generous character for print and screen.
Many OpenType features including 324 ligatures, contextuel alternates, and stylistic set built into all cuts.

I've been in a vintage-meets-modern mood in my most recent font construction, and this is no exception. Whiskey Tango is a fun retro-style tall and narrow sans-serif font with a scoop of variety: it includes over 110 items in the Private Use Area, including small caps, alternates, ligatures, and ordinal indicators. 

As usual for me, this font contains over 300 extended Latin characters for language support, as well as full uppercase and lowercase sets of Greek and Cyrillic characters.

Westsac, a perky little Roman-influenced free font that will add levity to your layouts while maintaining a traditional classic style that’s easily accessible to your readers. Westsac is named after WEST SACramento, home to a lady who came up to Chank and started telling him about how she had just decked her husband because she found out he was cheating with another lady and then she asked for a ride back home to her home in West Sac. Yeah, right.

This font was created at a fontmaking workshop that was hosted by Chank Diesel with the Sacramento Art Directors and Artists Club.

Wesna references the letterings of Slovenian posters and their typographic legacy. The interwar period posters took on an important role in public communication and became part of the public space or, so to speak, the street, by which they influenced the everyday life. 
Letterforms are narrow so that more text can be used on poster sizes. Horizontal terminals, sharp diagonal joints and super carismatic italics contribute to unique characterstics of Wesna. Including 3 weights with additional italics, stylistic sets within Latin and Cyrillic script.

Inspired by early grotesque typefaces such as Akzidenz Grotesk and Venus, Werksatz is our contemporary interpretation of this beloved genre. With 10 weights from Thin to Black, each with matching obliques and more than 940 characters, this font family is ready for the future. Special glyphs like three variations of arrows and additional shapes will make your design work so much easier. Among a treasure trove of OpenType features, you’ll find advanced functions like Small Caps, Subscript and Inferior figures and letters, plenty figure sets, etc. Werksatz is less formalistic and rigid than your average neogrotesk typeface, championing the corporate world as well as culture, fashion, and art.

Werkdruck is a serif typeface from the good old times made fit for our day, threading together different sources of rational and transitional type design. A sturdy construction makes reading copy easy, while the decidedly digital curves show their strength in large sizes. Unlike its narrower turn-of-the-century predecessors, Werkdruck opts for more generous shapes with contemporary digital needs in mind, remaining legible when set small on high-resolution displays. The 9 weights of the Werkdruck family come with true italics and sport 911 glyphs each—all you need for complex typesetting. Werkdruck is the ideal serif companion for our popular sans, Werksatz.

Developed out of a desire for my own workhorse text face & also taking cues from my display type inklings, my eponymous font can do a lot very credibly. There’s almost too much variability. Almost.

If you look closely, you’ll find a wide range of influences, from the deep cuts of House’s Paperback to the quirk of Mark Simonson’s Proxima Nova, to even the raw lines of Base Sans. And yes, I did just list the three most influential fonts in my own design career. I have tried to infuse features of some of these, among many other faces in creating what I’m proud to call by my name.

Waypointer is a symbol font with arrows.

The arrows are accessed with the standard keyboard keys. Use uppercase (A to Z) and lowercase (a to z) for pre-made arrows that point right, left, up, or down. Make your own arrow of any length with the 1 to 9 keys. The arrow sizes match the standard cap height of most fonts. 

OpenType features include, stylistic sets for changing arrow directions in 360 degree angles and stylistic alternates for quick changes between pointing right and left.

It has a few extras such as a map pin, anchor, and lightning bolt. These are included and accessed with the comma, period, and zero keys.

The origins of Wayfarer lie the Granby typeface developed by Stephenson Blake during the 1930s; itself reminiscent of the Underground typeface designed by Edward Johnston. Wayfarer develops elements of this face, but also some of the idiosyncratic qualities seen in the grotesque types of the latter half of the 19th century. There are some niche details such as the diamond dot over the i and j, and superior capitals – included as a nod to a piece of period typography, where superior small capitals appear in contractions on old street signs and company names. The family consists of 12 fonts with a character set that allows for detailed typography across a wide range of languages.

With the trace of the letterpress process elegantly stylized as a touch of distress, Shinn gives the lie to Eric Gill’s assertion that letters are things, not pictures of things. And in sustaining ambiguity between type as picture and type as thing, he achieves a wistful grace that is both formally and emotionally evocative.

name: Virus VujaDe
authors: Jonathan Barnbrook, James Lunn, Julián Moncada, Daniel Streat

raw.designer: Jonathan Barnbrook, James Lunn, Julián Moncada, Daniel Streat
raw.description: Virus VujaDe generates sequentially alternating glyphs. A remix project that draws directly from the extended glyph palettes of the Open source DejaVu fonts. It combines analphabetic glyphs, foreign scripts and symbols to create a palette of 4 alternate characters of each letter/number in Latin and Cyrillic alphabets. The result is a new font giving unexpected juxtapositions as the user types. It was designed as a key element of the visual identity for the first Kyiv Biennale of contemporary art, Arsenale 2012. This font is released under the same open-source license as the original DejaVu, allowing derivative works (as long as Bitstream or Vera are not in the names), and redistribution.

name: Virus DejaVu Serif
authors: Jonathan Barnbrook, James Lunn, Julián Moncada, Daniel Streat

raw.designer: Jonathan Barnbrook, James Lunn, Julián Moncada, Daniel Streat
raw.description:
Virus DejaVu is based on the collaborative open-source project DejaVu. It includes a including sans-serif, serif and monospace. It is a development of Bitstream Vera, originally designed by Jim Lyles in 2002. During the development of Virus DejaVu, the 13 weights of the original DejaVu were manually respaced and certain characters redrawn.
This font is a key element of the visual identities for the Ukrainian cultural centre, Mystetskyi Arsenal and for the first Kyiv international biennale of contemporary art, Arsenale 2012. Virus DejaVu is released under the same open-source license, allowing derivative works (as long as Bitstream or Vera are not in the names), and full redistribution.

This Devanagari display typeface is an extension of a lettering piece we designed for the title of the book– Drukchintan (दृक्‌चिंतन). A compilation of contemplative and critical essays on works of 31 modern artists from India and across the world, Drukchintan is authored by contemporary painter and art teacher Prabhakar Kolte. True to the spirit of Modern art, this typeface breaks away from tradition and experiments with the visual form of the Devanagari script. Robust shapes interspersed with delicate outlines give the typeface it’s unusual texture. While the solid rectangles and circles of the Dandas (दंड) and Bindus (बिंदू) dominate the visual space, the thin lines define character shapes; a fine

Roll over, Lance Wyman, and tell Bridget Riley the news. Designed by an old hippy for maximum dazzle, Vibro is an ice cream headache of a typeface which exploits the principles of chromatic vibration to send streams of high voltage through the viewer’s visual cortex. In the interest of greater stripiness, counters have been dispensed with. A selection of dingbats add to the ruckus. A full range of diacritics has been mortised into the bodies of the letters, enabling Vibro to trample basic standards of legibility in over 130 languages.

Vesper is designed to effortlessly set large amounts of text that is comfortable to read. It quietly exudes unique personalities in both text and display sizes yet remains unobtrusive to the reading process. The family consists of five weights & italics which contain wide language support. There are many OpenType features for complex typographic tasks for everything from fine book or magazine typesetting to academic and academic texts. Vesper has many contextual alternates that utilize subtly altered versions of letters, along with slightly customized spacing. This results in a more even gray on the page with enhanced legibility and a more comfortable reading experience.

Vena Amoris, or “Vein of Love” refers to the fourth finger on the left hand which was traditionally believed to contain a vein running directly to the heart, hence “the ring finger.”

As a digital font, Vena Amoris boasts an extensive Latin-based glyph repertoire that supports 208 languages. Also included are stylistic and contextual alternates, ligatures, swash variants, oldstyle figures, automatic roman numerals, and embellished words, imbuing a vivacious quality and grace to any setting. All of those extra goodies are driven by cleverly engineered OpenType features allowing you to easily bring harmony and beauty into your layouts.

Tall. Narrow. Spaced wide. Sounds like a pair of fashionable trousers to me! Named after a song by the band Propellerheads, this font is fun for crafts, print, branding, and more!

Not only are there standard letters, but the font also contains alternates for all uppercase letters with fun swirls on top of them. Use them for emphasis, or for an entire word!

The font comes with the basic A-Z and a-z alphabet sets; numbers 0-9; basic Latin punctuation; double-letter ligatures for EE, ee, TT, tt; stylistic alternates for E, e, and t; and the swirly party alternates for the uppercase set, mapped to the swash OpenType function.

Velocity is an all-caps, attention-grabbing sans serif, ready to accelerate across the starting line with horizontally tight letterforms that prioritise compactness without becoming cramped. Its high degree of curvature and forward momentum make it ideal for branding and contemporary design, shining when set in large type. With 12 stylistic sets and three sets of diacritics, Velocity easily adapts to different design environments. All 7 weights are duplexed, allowing quick switches from Thin to ExtraBold when sprinting towards the end-line.

For years, I’ve walked by several of these “Vault Alarm” boxes on the side of old New England banks. “Someday, I’d love to turn that lettering into a font”, I’d say. I finally made that a reality!

Vault Alarm is a chunky, quirky, display sans-serif I designed based on those handful of letters. It’s all-caps with numbers and basic punctuation—plus a few bonus alternate characters (G, Z, #, &). It comes in Regular (sharp) and Soft (subtly-rounded) which are both included.

 I can’t wait to see what you design with it.

Varese Gradient is a color font for display, headlines, or large body text. Use it for bold graphic statements or a vintage mood. Its geometric style is inspired by Art Deco and early 1900s European travel posters.

This typeface will set a friendly tone while making messages unique and memorable.

The gradients transition vertically and come in these sets; color with white, color with black, two colors, chromatic grays, grayscales, and concepts like summer and cappuccino. The font name will indicate its color. The full family includes one regular font.

The lowercase letters are cap high with counterforms and variations on certain glyphs (H/h, E/e, F/f, I/i, J/j, L/l, N/n, T/t).

Varese is a geometric and modular typeface inspired by early 1900s Art Deco posters. 

It is excellent for display use. The lowercase letters are cap high with counterforms and variations on certain glyphs (H/h, E/e, F/f, I/i, J/j, L/l, N/n, T/t). The lowercase also includes two alternate glyph sets that are half the size and align with the cap height. One of the alternate glyph sets features an underline, while the other does not.

VanSans is a humanist sans family, created to bring a fun and warm spirit into a minimalistic design. It was inspired by the city of Vancouver, merging an industrial feel with the friendliness and openness of its people. Featuring a large x-height and open counters, it’s clear and legible in both print and screen environments. The family is designed to be flexible and adapt to any typographic hierarchy a designer will need. With weights ranging from Thin to Black, it supports both extended Latin and Cyrillic with multiple OpenType features. VanSans works best in editorial, web branding and advertising – and is ready to be challenged by you.

Valvolina is a bold headline font inspired by Italian Futurism and the Moderne graphic design of the inter-war period. It uses elementary geometric shapes to build its characters, lending it an energy and punch. Dramatic and contemporary.

Urby melts dynamic shapes with geometric construction for branding and editorial. 
The different weights and styles share identical character widths, allowing you to change the weight or style of text without having to worry about text reflow — ideal for interface design. And despite being eye catching at display sizes, Urby works surprisingly well for short text.
Extremely wide apertures, like in a, e or s, and organic stroke endings (v, x) bring playfulness to Urby’s geometric construction and reduced shapes (t, f, 4) and quirky details underscore Urby’s unique character. Its rich character set supports most Latin languages and provides helpful dingbats and geometric shapes.

Urbane Rounded is a curved, friendly version of Urbane, a versatile all-purpose sans-serif family of six weights plus italics.

It explores the same idea-space as early geometric modernist sans such as Futura, Erbar, Spartan and Elegant Sans, with a single-story a, a contemporary high x-height and very slightly condensed bowls.

Perfect for headlines and running text, it is clear, classic and authoritative. Unusually for a geometric moderne sans, letter-widths are optically balanced, giving an even colour in setting. Includes a full international character set, lining, tabular and old-style numerals.

Urbane Condensed is an addition to the popular Urbane series, a versatile all-purpose sans-serif family of six weights plus italics. 

Perfect for headlines and running text, it is clear, classic and authoritative. Urban Circus is a big, grand display font that celebrates both the thoughtful, carefully constructed elements of contemporary urban planning and also the joyful, chaotic and magical elements of the circus. This typeface comes in four font styles which have a total of eight different alphabets that can be used together to create dramatic poster headlines and titles. Use the different alphabets on overlapping layers in different colors for a striking poster effect.

Joachim Müller-Lancé’s Uppercut Angle is a rather sporting fellow, inspired by the popular self-defense system Krav Maga. The design’s shapes are not calligraphic or handwritten, but more like lettering seen in comics or sports logos. Its brush movements are imagined, not literal. During development, details were simplified and reduced until a cut-paper feel had emerged, but more fluid like writing. Uppercut Angle is decidedly analog, muscular but not bulky, with the fluid, determined movements of a boxer or martial artist — not theatrical but powerful, confident, and dynamic. In the proportions, there is emphasis on the upper edge while some stems duck below the baseline.

Univerza Sans was developed to mark the hundredth anniversery of University of Ljubljana. The style is influenced by the combination of Slovenian avantgarde with some recognizable forms that are known for Slovenian typography. Multifunctional use for identity system, formal communication, wayfinding, academic and scientific articles in order to share the institution’s spirit of knowledge, creativity, diversity and belonging. It speaks Central European languages, feels official but looks attractive and recognizable.

Unicaster is a grotesque typeface with a unified case height for both upper and lower case. This style, known as Unicase, provides a strong composition appropriate for short texts, titles, packaging and similar forms that fall into the ‘Display’ category.

The original reference to the typography is found on the back cover of the album Part One by the psychedelic group West Coast Pop Art Experimental Band (WCPAEB), published in 1967, where the extensive name of the group appears written in these characters with an irresistible charm. 

We did some research on the original font and, finding no clues, we decided to offer our personal view of the model.

Uni Neue is the newly redesigned version of Uni Sans—one of the signature font families of Fontfabric Type Foundry. With significant changes like proportions, widths, and thickness, this new family lets us feel and understand the font at a whole new level.

Uni Neue represents modern sans serif typefaces with a distinctive character and geometric feel. The rounded corners give the typeface a friendly look, yet it retains a professional quality suitable for corporate branding both on and off the screen.

Muller supports a wide range of languages, including Extended Latin, Cyrillic, and Greek. The family has seven weights, ranging from Thin to Black, with corresponding Italics.

Uncle Grump is based on one of the styles people want the most when I'm doing hand-lettered projects. It's heavy and bold, but rounded on the corners and has a fun hand-drawn feel. It's great for all your kid-related projects, but can also fit with a grown-up vibe.

Plus, because I like to give you options, I've included some extras -- by layering the same words on top of each other and changing each layer's font, you can add in some dots, an outline, or both! And as usual, I've smoothed the lines and reduced the number of nodes/points to make this a clean font for crafting.

Halfway between nineteenth century display wood letters and the Scotch Romans, we can find Ultramarina, a novelty serif font for use in large body headlines, which shows its power of attraction to quality food, the country’s legume, and gentlemen with a mustache and apron.

Ultramarina has been revamped in 2025 with a better design and wider language coverage.

Typold originated out of the desire to improve, geometric forms and push beyond previous achievements through collaborative working methods and knowledge sharing. The result is a finely balanced modern sans serif constructed from mathematical inputs, typographers needs, and the natural hand and eye of an artisan. Details include eight weights and matching italics, three separate widths, 1000 characters with an alternative lowercase a and y, small-caps, 12 variations of numerals, Opentype features inferiors, superiors, fractions, case sensitive punctuation, extended symbols including emoji's and language support covering Western, South and Central Europe.

Inspired by the London foundry Stephenson Blake typeface Blackfriars, designer extraordinaire Roberto de Vicq de Cumptich reimagined this quirky gem for today. de Vicq brought a more graceful appearance to the design and explored its reversed contrast nature with new weights, while still retaining the warmth and character of its English primogenitor of the Victorian era. The proportions of the lowercase are decidedly wider and more geometric overall. Tuppence includes a marvelous selection of catch words, swash capitals, ligatures, arrows, and over a hundred beautiful ornaments. Picture Tuppence used on beverage labels, greeting cards, posters, restaurant logos, and in other display mediums.
Casual informal handwriting font

Tropical Punch is a retro-tropical font with a ton of variety: I've included nearly 200 multi-letter ligatures with nesting letters, to add quirky and fun variety to all of your projects.  There are also a few alternate vowels, plus a few dingbats to add jazzy pizzazz; and 10 smaller catchwords like THE, AND, WITH, and more!

I've also made an outline version--Tropical Punch Outline--which surrounds the solid letters beautifully, so you have even more options! Of course, both versions have my usual 300+ extended Latin characters for language support. And I've included a set of uppercase Greek letters as well!

Trilogy Sans explores the ‘designer cool’ aesthetic of the grotesque style of types that grew and developed to become the backbone of graphic design. A style of type which is celebrated for being systematic, neutral, functional and to some degree invisible. Perfectly capable of setting text beautifully. From setting headlines and continuous text to finer aspects such as map detailing and tabular information; Trilogy Sans excels with its typographic variety. One of its many strengths is the inclusion of several alternate letters that deliver an instant change to the typographic image. As part of the larger Trilogy family it harmonises well, with Trilogy Egyptian and Trilogy Fatface.

Trilogy Fatface is exuberant. It may only have one heavy weight and only be in italic, but this gives it the opportunity to flaunt itself across the page. It sketches out from a regular width to an audacious and bouncy ultra-expanded. The character set includes a full set of swash capitals as well as an expanded range of lowercase swashes. All this and small capitals, ligatures, and extensive number sets; Trilogy Fatface can bring a huge amount of spirit and joy to a piece of typographic design. As part of the wider Trilogy family it shares certain details, and  harmonises well with Trilogy Sans and Trilogy Egyptian.

Trilogy Egyptian is a strong chunky set of fonts in three width families. It commands attention and is great when you want to make your presence felt, and where room allows. Even though the letters are quite static and simplistic in structure, they manage to exert an impressive amount of personality. This is achieved through the use of deep cuts. The accompanying italic benefits from various calligraphic touches which impart a strong horizontal flow to the setting. Capitals create an impressive typographic image in their own right. As part of the wider Trilogy family it shares certain details, and harmonises well, with Trilogy Sans and Trilogy Fatface.

There are three widths, all of which have bold chunky weights. As part of the wider Trilogy family it shares certain details, and harmonises well, with Trilogy Sans and Trilogy Fatface.

Trevor is a narrow, sturdy slab serif — both heavy and kind — arousing sympathy for the subject at hand. It connects with others by consciously riding the line between being personal and commanding, inky and rounded.

Tragic Grotesk is a sans serif family for branding and editorial. It references early 20th century Grotesk styles in letters and forms such as G and g. Slightly bend diagonal in k, v, w etc. add playfulness and a human touch. Straight shapes in round glyphs hint to DIN-esque typefaces. This mix of influences melds into a spirited family of eight weights from Thin to Ultra plus some fun icons inspired by the typeface name: Tragic. Eight slanted styles complete the family.

name: Traction
authors: Christian Thalmann, Miriam Surányi, Chiara Mattersdorfer

raw.designer: Christian Thalmann, Miriam Surányi, Chiara Mattersdorfer
raw.description: Swiss astronomer Christian Thalmann originally designed Traction. This typeface sports signature serifs, soft edges, and a fluid, organic design. If we look at it in detail, the organic letters are reminiscent of the profiles of ­off-road tires and hiking boots. In small text sizes, it is the humanistic forms that set the tone to ensure fluid legibility. Totaling 18 styles in nine weights, all fonts come with small capitals and all possible numerical variations.

Tourette draws inspiration from 19th century French lightweight slab serifs, an under-explored area, full of beautiful, sensitive fonts. It comes in two versions: Normal – simple, delicate and legible, and Extreme full of little flourishes that give an exquisite, slightly frivolous, feel bordering on the manic. The controversial choice of name originates from one of the prevailing themes in the work of Barnbrook Fonts: the power of language. This nod to ‘obscenity in polite company’ provides both a direct contrast to the delicacy of the letterforms and the almost whimsical sounding name ‘Tourette’.

Torque is a modern sans serif inspired by classic athletic, space exploration, video-game and sci-fi movie lettering styles. It has a soft, yet stern, look capable of representing nearly everything from traditional sports to advanced technology. In addition to the standard letter forms, each style in the family has an enormous set of highly stylized alter ego alternates that instantly give the text an unmistakably hyper-futuristic appearance.

Tome Sans was created to be an inconspicuous sans-serif that performs beautifully across multiple environs. Tome Sans does not bring attention to itself and it does subscribe to trends; rather, it is a more timeless design. Tome Sans has 10 weights ranging from ExtraThin to Black with companion italics and boasts a glyph repertoire of 875 glyphs. Among those glyphs are several sets of numerals (including Tabular and Oldstyle figures), arrows, and a trove of letters spanning several complete Unicode® ranges supporting 224 languages. In addition, a host of thoughtful but unobtrusive OpenType features are built in and ready to assist in setting your composition — a valuable toolset addition.

All the things you love about Swiss style typography but with more hang loose attitude. The Swiss International Style was a movement in typography that aimed to create order. It was buttoned-up, straight-laced, and a bit pompous if we’re being honest. Tofino’s letterforms are inspired by the Neo-Grotesque typefaces of that time but with some buttons undone and some laces a little wiggly. 

The design is inspired by small, descriptive labeling text used throughout an old type specimen. Tofino is a slightly squared, condensed workhorse family that is well-suited to a screen environment. TJ Evolette A is unique, customizable, experimental, fashionable and clean. This geometric, grotesque and all-caps display family has seven weights, one basic glyph set, two integrated and extravagant stylistic sets for the whole alphabet and some astonishing special characters.
Between the basic glyph set and the two stylistic sets, the typeface offers innumerable combination possibilities. In its two sets of alternate characters interpretations of Art Deco mingle with the straight lines of ancient runes. This variety encourages striking editorial and poster design.
Without OpenType support we recommend ‘TJ Evolette A Mix’. A version with a no-hassle, predefined mix of some of special glyph

In my house, we refer to typing with just the index fingers of each hand "tippy tappy typing." I'm not good with my thumbs, so if I have to type on my phone, I prefer to set it down flat and tippy tappy type on it.

Thus, when I decided to draw a font that's typewriter-ish, the name seemed perfect!

This one was all draw by hand, then cleaned up so it will both print and cut well. And to make things even more fun, I drew a set of almost 100 bonus items: doodles, shapes, squiggles, swirls, arrows, and catchwords of "and" and "the".  They're included in the separate "Tippy Tappy Dingbats" font file.

Tippy Tappy Type includes 300+ extended Latin characters, and some alternates too!

Timonium is a distinctive high-contrast sans serif typeface designed for use in medium to enormous sizes. The family was inspired by a lettering style that appears throughout modern design history on cereal boxes, jazz album covers, pharmaceutical advertisements, stereophonic sound systems, action movie titles, and, most recently, athletic and automobile racing logos. Timonium contains five weights with italics, all with small caps and other features.

Inspired by LED displays, Ticker has a technological precision. Though the modular character of the elements suggests digital displays, the letters are carefully crafted, spaced, and kerned: they offer the feel of older or simpler technology, but they are more polished and functional than common, crude pixel fonts. In addition to electronic signage, the typeface evokes video games, Lite-Brite toys, ceramic tile signage, marquee lights, or vintage tickertape.

A stencil has a physical body. Depending on several factors, it could be paper-thin or heavy as a board. Stencils are often used to create intermediate steps that help make marks on other surfaces. You can also create signage with stencils. 
One of the best ways to make a stencil is with a laser-cutter. Luc(as) modified letter shapes for type size and material thickness. How small can you go before the bridges burn?
Bridges serve several purposes: they keep the countershapes from falling out, they stabilize complex shapes, and they are actually design elements themselves. The spaces between characters, shapes, and diacritics are never smaller than the bridge width.

TheSerif is part of the Thesis superfamily. Although it was conceived to be the perfect secondary font within the Thesis system – for use in headlines, subheads, pull quotes, etc. – TheSerif has also been used successfully as a text font in its own right.

Luc(as) developed TheSans Typewriter as an independent version of TheSans Mono, which would allow designers to simulate the appearance of typewritten text in print and on-screen. The typefaces’ design elements are sharp, and the content produced with them are sympathetic and have personality. Like TheSans Mono, all the characters in TheSans Typewriter are monospaced – both within the family’s three weights and across those weights, too.
TheSans is a modern classic. A favourite for corporate design, editorial design and new media, it comes in an astounding range of widths and weights, including a large set of hairline fonts.
TheSans Mono is a monospaced version of TheSans.

TheMix is a semi-serif typeface with low-contrast – i.e., the differences between thin and thick strokes are not very pronounced. Yet the reference to writing with the broad-nibbed pen is still present, giving the letters a diagonal stress and a forward flow that facilitates reading.
TheMix Mono is a monospaced version of TheMix.

TheAntiqua Sun was originally made as a corporate typeface for Sun Microsystems; it has sharper details and a simpler structure than other variants of TheAntiqua and is limited to two weights, Regular and Bold.

Although the members of the Thesis family have proven to work well as text faces, nothing beats a medium-contrast oldstyle for comfortable immersive reading. Hence TheAntiqua, an all-purpose text face whose name refers to the traditional Dutch/German word for oldstyle.

This font has heavy roots in one of my favorite lettering styles. It's rough, scrappy, and likes to do its own thing. It has a full uppercase and lowercase set, numbers, punctuation, and lots of extended Latin characters for language support. It also includes alternate versions of 17 lowercase letters.

Where Terrapin really shines is in the ligatures. I've written separate two- and three-letter combined forms for some of the most common letter combinations, and a few uncommon ones to boot. There are almost 100 ligatures in here, all PUA-encoded so everyone can access them (and also coded so if your software does automatic ligature replacement, they'll pop right in).

Teramo™ is daring, sharp and dynamic. Its personality is derived from asymmetry and movement. It is a contemporary serif family full of modern design elements playing with proportions of works of XV and XVI century masters such as Francesco Griffo or Claude Garamond.

The family features four optical sizes. Display sizes feature extreme stroke contrast and are intended for fashion, lifestyle, cosmetics, magazine, business, hi-tech and advertising use. Text styles are created for all kinds of body copy — long and short paragraphs, books and websites in any modern design context. They are crafted to be elegant and legible, featuring more generous spacing and scrupulous kerning.

Tenso is an economic running sans serif with a lot of character. It carries some hints of grotesque such a one-story lowercase g and closed, angled strokes on C, G and S. On the other hand it has a higher than normal stroke contrast and also a real italic (not only sloped). This balanced mix makes it a playful grotesque sans suitable for all kinds of publications, apps, and websites.

When we trimmed the serifs off our new slab serif family Mortise, we found a plain, efficient sans that marches through the uncanny valley between grotesk and geometric, with almost circular bowls that lend extra energy to the line. Like its sibling, Tenon has open counters, a generous x-height, and wide proportions that suit both small sizes and bold headlines.

Look at these big loud fancy letters! Ben Eine is one of London’s most prolific and original street artists who specialises in the central element of all graffiti — the form of letters. So it’s only natural that his work should be adapted to become a font for modern age computers. So Chank Diesel worked with Eine to create TENDERLOIN. Tenderloin comes in two beautiful styles that can be overlapped. The uppercase are the fills, and the lowercase are the shadows; set them in different colors on overlapping text blocks and voila! you get thrilling two-color type!

Based in English lettering traditions, Temeraire rescues disparate styles from echoes in time. This serif font family is meant for beholding text in books, magazines, and large formats rather than being able to ignore it.

Although the Taz family was designed for newspapers, it works equally well in many other contexts. The fonts have been used in glossy magazines, sales catalogues and corporate brochures, for instance. Taz is appreciated for its readability in longer texts at medium sizes. Since its inception, the Taz typeface has steadily been expanded. The current version comes in a staggering range of 15 weights, including a large series of distinctive hairline fonts and an UltraBlack for maximum impact on giant posters and in magazine headlines.

Taxon is a straightlined Sans with a clean, fresh and unsentimental look. Related to classical faces like Optima and Imago, it appears more contemporary and merges the austere linearity of the Grotesk with the elegance of the Antiqua.

The Taxon family consists of 12 styles and is well suited for ambitious typography. It comes in OpenType format with extended language support. All weights contain ligatures, superior characters, proportional lining figures, tabular lining figures, proportional old style figures, lining old style figures, matching currency symbols, fraction- and scientific numerals, matching arrows and alternate characters.

Taüll is inspired by old black lettering devices. Its main goal is to link the medieval world with our brand new digital smart cities. A southern flavored typeface that transfers us to the heart of the Pyrenees mountains, with its tiny villages, Romanesque churches, old huts, and dark forests with dragons and princesses. An idyllic vision of life from the mountain slow pace where cattle graze on the open meadows and birds sing. Those lost paradises that we can revive thanks to the natural flavor of Taüll’s character outlines.

Dan Milne first conceived Tasman as a typeface for newspapers. This influenced the proportions and look of the face considerably: the goal was to keep the personality as warm and playful as possible without losing the credible tone required to deliver all kinds of news.
A sturdy, warm type family that is neither mechanical nor fragile. It borrows its name from Abel Janszoon Tasman (1603–1659), a Dutch seafarer, explorer, and merchant who mapped parts of Australia in 1642, including Van Diemen’s Land (now known as Tasmania). Tasman’s primary purpose is an unbiased presentation of information; it strives for neutrality over elegance.

Searching for the Exceptional.

Designing Tapir was driven by the search for a display typeface which is doing something different than the rounded and bouncy fun faces – the letterforms should stand out with a slight touch of weirdness, creating attention and recognizabilty. A big character set, optimized spacing & kerning and lots of features make Tapir a good choice for professional usage between games, toys and skateboards.

The playful Tao family is bound to woo the hearts of math fans. The Unicode consortium defined code points for mathematical double-struck upper and lowercase letters, and when Luc(as) designed some of them for his TheAntiqua family, he was so pleased with the result that he turned it into a completely new family with 7 weights and real italics. Accented letters come in two variations; standard accents are single strokes, and when your linguistic needs rise, you can choose big open accents by activating a stylistic set. Meet Tao, a luscious serif font where all the thick strokes are built with double lines.

Tabulamore is a monospaced script typeface with two goals: to make a script face that looks as natural as possible within the limitation of monospace and to offer a better all-cap solution where many script typefaces fail to address. The typeface style is generally a loosely spaced casual script, whose spacing allows big letters like M W m to fit comfortably. The small cap part is based on the Architect’s Casual style and shows up automatically depending on the context.

As the name suggests, it is perfect for someone who likes to express their affection in a monospace format. It is available in the rough version and clean version.

Tabrizi Jali is a type revival in the Persian Naskh style based on the 19th-century fount of type produced by Mirza Zayn-ol-Abedin Tabrizi in Tehran. In 1827, this type was used to publish the earliest known Qur’an printed with movable type in a Muslim country. For the history of the original foundry type see: Borna Izadpanah, 2023, ‘Persian and Arabic printing with movable type in Qajar Iran (1818–1900)’, in Arabic Typography: History and Practice, Salenstein: niggli, 75–22. https://www.niggli.ch/en/produkt/arabic-typography/

Sybarite is a fat face that works at any size. Capitals with sweeping curves and sharp unbracketed serifs command attention while charming minuscules expose the amiable side of its demeanor.

Sybarite is James Puckett’s revival of the fat face type that appears in the 1829 specimen of Alonzo W. Kinsley’s Franklin Letter Foundry.

With a swooshy hand-painted flow, the strokes of this vintage brush script will make your designs sing and dance. While each character is charming on its own merit, put 'em together and this font dances with the swing rhythm and bursting energy of Benny Goodman’s big band. And don't miss the dandy special characters for letter combinations tt, th, or, os, and an extra fancy alternate capital M.


Without a doubt, Swingdancer will satisfy the script jones of any retro font fan.

Mario De Libero designed Swanstone while investigating XIX Century Old Style typefaces. Designs like Theophile Beaudoire’s Romana (1860) or Miller & Richard’s Modernized Old Style, that re-imagined the classical “Venetian” letterforms adding flared serifs and early Art Nouveau influences. In Italy, one of these fonts was Raffaello Bertieri’s Raffaello, which De Libero used as the starting point of his research in a contemporary retelling of these exuberant and sexily unsettling letterforms.

This typeface family, inspired by Norse mythology and Scandinavian Architecture, draws a bridge between a The character set will allow text layouts to have this unusual corkiness which make it so particular and so comfortable to read. The rounded glyphs’ width are shaped in such a way that they operate a discrete rupture in the text rhythmic.
